name: Best of all possible worlds / theodicy
plain_explanation: Leibniz argued that before creating anything, God considered infinitely many possible worlds and chose to create the one with the greatest excess of good over evil - so even though our world contains evil, it is nonetheless the best world logically possible, because some goods (like free will) cannot exist without the risk of some evils (like sin).
precise_definition: The doctrine that a possible world is one not contradicting the laws of logic; God, being good, necessarily creates the possible world with the greatest surplus of good over evil, so the evils that exist are logically necessary for a greater compensating good and provide no argument against God's goodness.
why_it_mattered: It was Leibniz's popular solution to the problem of evil, satisfying enough to please royal patrons like the Queen of Prussia, but Russell judges it 'logically possible, but not very convincing.'
historical_origin: Set out in the Theodicee and the Monadology; famously satirized by Voltaire as the philosophy of Dr. Pangloss, and mocked by F. H. Bradley's remark that 'everything in it is a necessary evil.'
examples: Free will is a great good, but it was logically impossible for God to grant free will while also decreeing there would be no sin, so God permitted Adam's fall as the price of a world with free will.
The comparison of a drink of cold water being more pleasurable after enduring thirst.
objections: Russell constructs a deliberately fantastic mirror-image argument (a Manichaean claim that this is the worst of all possible worlds) to show Leibniz's argument is no more rigorous than its opposite.
Russell notes the argument conveniently comforted the Queen of Prussia while her serfs continued to suffer real evil.
competing_positions: A Manichaean view that the world is designed by a wicked demiurge to maximize suffering, given as a parallel fantastic argument by Russell
influence_on_later_thinkers: Voltaire's Doctor Pangloss in Candide is a direct satire of Leibniz's popular optimism.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Written to reassure a queen; Russell notes it functioned to justify the comfort of the powerful amid the suffering of their subjects.
